The hook Producer Laurie Borg called it the "anti-Downton Abbey" — the "secret history of England" told through working-class Birmingham rather than aristocracy. That ambition drives its media language, representations and industrial identity.

M Media Language

Genre, technical & visual codes, intertextuality and narrative structure — how S1E1 builds meaning.

Genre — crime/gangster, hybridised (NICS)

Identify genre through Narrative, Iconography, Characters and Setting. Peaky Blinders is a crime drama that hybridises the gangster film with the western and the period/costume drama.

  • Iconography: flat caps, three-piece tweed suits, guns, horses, cobbled streets, the Garrison pub, and fire / furnaces in almost every scene — an industrial, "hellish" Birmingham.
  • Technical & audio codes: low-key lighting, slow motion, and the anachronistic rock soundtrack — Nick Cave's "Red Right Hand" — build a mythic, stylised tone. This is verisimilitude within a heightened diegesis.
  • Neale — repetition & difference: recognisable gangster conventions (family loyalty, threatened power) give repetition; the Birmingham setting, PTSD backstory and rock score give difference. Genres are dynamic and historically relative.

Intertextuality

Audiences take pleasure in recognising references — meaning is created in the decoding. S1E1 draws on the gangster canon:

Also the Western (Tommy's ride down Watery Lane; townsfolk hiding) and a literary nod to T.S. Eliot's "The Waste Land" — fragmentation echoing Tommy's post-war psyche.

Narrative

  • Todorov: the episode opens with an already-disrupted equilibrium (Tommy's stolen guns bring Campbell to Birmingham). Little is resolved — only the horse race — typical of long-form drama.
  • Flexi-narrative: multiple interweaving arcs (the guns, Campbell, Grace the undercover barmaid, Danny's PTSD/"death", Ada & Freddie) build richness; open-ended rather than closed.
  • Restricted & unrestricted narration: we largely follow Tommy, but we know more than the characters (Grace's true identity, Danny's staged death) — creating enigma codes (Barthes) and dramatic irony.

Baudrillard & the postmodern reading Peaky Blinders can be read as postmodern through anachronism (contemporary music in 1919), bricolage and pastiche of gangster/western texts, intertextuality, and the fragmented self of Tommy. The stylised, mediated 1919 becomes a hyper-reality / simulacrum — "more real" than the history it depicts.
Exam question seen in class"How far can Peaky Blinders be defined as post-modern? [15]" — argue both sides: hybridity/pastiche/anachronism vs its rootedness in real history and social realism.

R Representation

How people, place and history are constructed through selection & combination (Hall) — via narrative positioning, performance, costume, framing and lighting.

Character representations

  • Tommy Shelby — the anti-hero. Cillian Murphy's performance is deliberately understated and static against the intense cast — the "strong, silent" Western archetype, coiled and ready. His PTSD backstory adds emotional depth. Labelling him an anti-hero frees the audience from having to sympathise.
  • Arthur — the less-smart, more-violent sibling: a stock gangster role and a binary opposition to Tommy.
  • Aunt Polly — the matriarch around whom the family's power orbits.
  • The women (Polly, Ada, Grace) — strong and empowered, reflecting the burst of female independence during WWI. Yet the world is heavily masculine (the office, the Garrison, the police hall) and Grace is told "what to expect" working in a bar.
  • Inspector Campbell — presents himself as cleaning out the "filth", but is revealed as hypocritical (police brutality; torturing Arthur). Low angles and fiery sermons construct his authority — the opposite of Tommy's stillness.

Representation of place & history

England is shown as darker, more violent and subversive than the sanitised costume-drama norm — no aristocracy, only the working class of one Birmingham district. This is historical revisionism: excavating the lives of the poor, women and migrants rather than royalty. Squalor is not downplayed, but the city is also a place of community, grudging respect and excitement.

Audience positioning We are aligned with the Shelbys over Campbell — through narrative positioning, Campbell's brutality, and the Churchill/Campbell talk of state-sanctioned assassination that frames Birmingham as lawless. We are, arguably, positioned to see violence as glamorous.
The oppositional reading Academic George Larke-Walsh: Peaky Blinders "glorifies violence, nationalist ideologies and toxic masculinity" — a key counter-argument for evaluation.

R Character Profiles — Stereotypes

Each character is built from a recognisable stock type, then given depth that conforms to or challenges the stereotype (Hall — constructed through selection & combination). Tap a portrait to enlarge.

Tommy Shelby

Cillian Murphy
The anti-hero / gang leader
✓ Conforms
  • The ambitious criminal who rises through violence and cunning to lead the family — the classic gangster protagonist.
  • Commands loyalty and fear; the "man of few words" who runs the operation.
✦ Challenges
  • Deliberately understated, still and silent — not the loud, brash mobster; the Western "strong, silent" archetype.
  • PTSD and vulnerability humanise him; intelligence over brute force. As an anti-hero we aren't obliged to approve of him.

Arthur Shelby

Paul Anderson
The volatile enforcer
✓ Conforms
  • The "less smart, more violent sibling" — the muscle of the gang and a stock gangster type.
  • Unstable and aggressive; a clear binary opposition to the controlled Tommy.
✦ Challenges
  • Emotional fragility, loyalty and his own war trauma give him real depth.
  • Capable of tenderness and breakdown — not a one-note thug.

Aunt Polly

Helen McCrory
The matriarch
✓ Conforms
  • The older matriarch around whom the family's power orbits — a recognisable crime-family role.
✦ Challenges
  • A powerful, feared, financially shrewd woman who ran the business while the men were at war — reflecting WWI female independence.
  • Challenges Van Zoonen's "women = domestic/passive" — she holds real authority in a masculine world.

Grace Burgess

Annabelle Wallis
Femme fatale / undercover agent
✓ Conforms
  • Introduced as "too pretty for the pub" — the beautiful barmaid and love interest, object of Tommy's gaze.
✦ Challenges
  • Revealed as a cunning undercover agent with her own mission and agency — active and deceptive, not a passive romantic prop.
  • Subverts the "sweet girl" first impression (unrestricted narration lets us in on the secret).

Inspector Campbell

Sam Neill
The lawman antagonist
✓ Conforms
  • The authoritative, determined lawman on a mission to clean out the "filth" of the city — righteous and forceful.
✦ Challenges
  • Subverts the "good cop": revealed as hypocritical and corrupt — police brutality, and torturing Arthur.
  • Constructed through low angles and fiery sermons as Tommy's binary opposite, so we side with the criminals.

Jeremiah Jesus

Benjamin Zephaniah · race & ethnicity
The preacher
✓ Conforms
  • Risks the marginalised / "pitied" or comic religious-outsider stereotype (Alvarado, Gutch & Wollen).
✦ Challenges
  • A respected, loyal member of the Shelby circle — a Black character woven naturally into 1919 working-class Birmingham.
  • Part of the show's "secret history" revisionism and a positive substitute image (Hall).
How to use this in the examDon't just describe a character — state the stock type, then evaluate how the construction (performance, costume, framing, narrative position) reinforces or subverts it, and link to a theorist (Hall, Gauntlett, Van Zoonen, bell hooks).

I Industry

Production, ownership, funding, distribution and regulation — a public-service broadcaster operating in a global market.

The BBC — Public Service Broadcasting

  • The BBC is a PSB: its aim is to benefit audiences, not profit. Lord Reith's ethos — "inform, educate and entertain."
  • Funded by the licence fee (£159 → collected by government → ~£3.7bn lump sum). No advertising, which protects impartiality.
  • BBC One remit: the most popular mixed-genre service, a wide range of high-quality programmes, a high proportion of original productions, reflecting the whole of the UK. Peaky Blinders' move to BBC One (S5–6) signals its status as a flagship drama.

Ownership, funding & vertical integration

  • Made by Caryn Mandabach Productions and Tiger Aspect with the BBC, and crucially co-funded by Screen Yorkshire (regional investment) — an example of the co-production model that spreads risk and raises production values.
  • The BBC is vertically integrated: BBC Studios produces in-house and distributes worldwide — striking co-production deals, building the brand globally, and selling programmes and formats.

Distribution in a global age

  • A "Netflix Original" in the US: one week before S2, Netflix acquired US rights from the Weinstein Company (2014), so it streams exclusively on Netflix there.
  • Global reach: Netflix in 183 countries, BBC iPlayer, Amazon Prime, DVD and iTunes; international distributors (Sky Germany, Entertainment One, Endemol). Convergence (streaming, mobile, VPNs) shrinks the world.
  • "Television is a global industry" — Peaky supports this through its multinational cast (Irish, Australian, European), universal themes (power, crime, family) and worldwide fanbase.

Scheduling & regulation

Originally 6 × 1hr, 9pm — a post-watershed slot for the crime genre (after EastEnders, before the News). S6 averaged 5.42m on Sunday BBC One. Regulated by Ofcom, with BBFC classification (the box set is an 18) and the watershed.

Marketing & Diversification

Hesmondhalgh: media companies use marketing and franchising to minimise risk and maximise audiences. Peaky is "sold" on stars, character, genre, intertextuality and BBC/Netflix quality.

Exam angle"Discuss how media organisations target audiences through marketing. Refer to Peaky Blinders." Link each item to a target: stars (Cillian Murphy), character (Tommy), genre (crime fans), intertextuality (Godfather fans), BBC/Netflix quality, plus the feature film, festival and fashion influence as diversification.

A Audience

How the text and its marketing target, reach and position audiences — and how audiences use, interpret and participate.

Categorising the audience

Producers categorise by socio-economic grade (A–E) and by values (VALs) — Young & Rubicam's Mainstreamers (~40%), Aspirers, Explorers, Succeeders and Reformers.

Primary

Fans of crime/gangster drama — mainstream, 15+ (18 on disc), broadly ABC1 "nostalgic crime".

Cross-gender

Male viewers identify with / aspire to the Shelby men; female viewers identify with Grace or find Tommy attractive.

Secondary / Tertiary

Fans of historical drama and of the 1920s period — the "hipster" flat-cap fashion; plus inherited fanbases (Boardwalk Empire) and star fans.

Using & interpreting the text

Blumler & Katz
Uses & Gratifications

Entertainment/diversion, relationships (fan communities), information (the era), identity (aligning with values). Plus nostalgia, escapism and catharsis.

Stuart Hall
Reception theory

Preferred: root for the Shelbys, violence as thrilling. Negotiated: enjoy it but uneasy. Oppositional: a feminist reading, or Larke-Walsh's "toxic masculinity".

Katz & Lazarsfeld
Two-step flow

Opinion leaders — critics, testimonials, BAFTA wins and the IMDb 8.8 (500k ratings) — shape responses before viewing.

Henry Jenkins
Fandom

Active, creative fans & textual poaching: fan fiction, fan art, wikis, the Peaky Blinders Festival, cosplay and the fan-sourced #PeakysFanArt campaign.

PositioningAudiences are positioned through VATs (visual, audio, technical codes) — camerawork aligns us with Tommy, visual codes immerse us in the era, and we feel dread for the Peakys who don't yet know Campbell has arrived.

C Contexts

The social, cultural, historical, political and economic circumstances that shape the product.

Historical

1919, just after WWI. Shell-shock / PTSD (Tommy, Danny), the burst of female independence during the war, and a real Birmingham gang that inspired the title.

Social & Cultural

Working-class industrial Birmingham — the "anti-Downton", a "secret history of England". We view 1919 through 21st-century eyes; the show's style even reshaped high-street fashion.

Political

Post-war unrest — the IRA, Communists, the state (Churchill) and class conflict frame the season's threats.

Economic / Institutional

PSB vs commercial funding; regional investment (Screen Yorkshire); and a global streaming market that a licence-fee broadcaster must compete in.

Theories — mapped to Peaky Blinders

Name them and evaluate — don't just label.

Media Language
Steve Neale — Genre

Repetition & difference; genres are dynamic, hybrid and historically relative.

Media Language
Todorov — Narratology

Equilibrium → disruption → recognition → repair → new equilibrium (here, largely unresolved).

Media Language
Lévi-Strauss — Structuralism

Binary oppositions (law/crime, Tommy/Campbell, English/Irish) drive the narrative.

Media Language
Baudrillard — Postmodernism

Hyper-reality, simulacra, anachronism, bricolage & pastiche.

Media Language
Barthes — Semiotics

Enigma/action codes; costume & setting as signs (the flat cap, fire).

Representation
Stuart Hall

Representation is constructed through codes; stereotypes stem from inequalities of power; "otherness".

Representation
David Gauntlett — Identity

A diverse range of characters lets audiences "pick and mix" identities.

Representation
Liesbet van Zoonen — Feminism

Gender is constructed; a "variety of feminist discourse"; femininity coded as care, masculinity as rationality.

Representation
bell hooks — Feminism

Patriarchy & the "ideology of domination"; class and race shape women's oppression, not gender alone.

Industry
Hesmondhalgh — Cultural Industries

Minimise risk & maximise audiences through franchises, stars and marketing.

Industry
Curran & Seaton

Power concentrated in a few profit-driven firms — evaluate against the BBC as a PSB.

Industry
Livingstone & Lunt — Regulation

Tension between citizen protection and consumer choice (Ofcom, watershed).

Audience
Blumler & Katz · Hall · Jenkins

Uses & gratifications, reception theory and fandom (see Audience above).

Exam essentials Component 2, Section A is 30 marks — a two-part question or one extended response across both TV set texts (Peaky Blinders + The Bridge). Practice questions from class:
  • "Explore how the representations in Peaky Blinders position audiences. [15]"
  • "'Television is a global industry.' To what extent does Peaky Blinders support this claim?"
  • "How far can Peaky Blinders be defined as post-modern? [15]"
  • "How might audiences respond differently to TV crime drama? Refer to Peaky Blinders. [15]"

Key Terms

Verisimilitude

The believability of the world of the characters — even a stylised world can feel "true".

Diegesis

The world in which the story takes place, including diegetic sound that characters can hear.

Flexi-narrative

Multiple interweaving story arcs across an episode/series, rather than one closed plot.

Anti-hero

A protagonist who lacks conventional heroic virtues — we follow Tommy without being obliged to approve of him.

Intertextuality

References to other media texts (The Godfather, The Untouchables); the pleasure lies in recognition.

Historical revisionism

Deliberately retelling a period through the lives of the poor, women and migrants rather than the elite.

Vertical integration

One company controls production and distribution — the BBC via BBC Studios.

PSB (Public Service Broadcasting)

Broadcasting funded to benefit audiences (inform, educate, entertain), not to make profit.

Watershed

The 9pm threshold before which UK broadcasters must not show adult content.

Textual poaching

(Jenkins) Fans taking elements of a text and reworking them — fan fiction, fan art, mashups.

Simulacrum / hyper-reality

(Baudrillard) A mediated image with no real origin that we accept as more "real" than reality.
